To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) we give the first lower bound for an explicitly given function in P, and (ii) we prove a general tradeoff between average-case hardness and formula size, and use this tradeoff to give a new lower bound for Andrev’s function, and to give non-trivial lower bounds for explicit candidate functions. 1
we show how to prove lower bounds for explicit simple functions, and we present candidates for such functions.
we prove a tight lower bound for formula size of explicit functions, and we give non-traditional explicit functions with large formula complexity.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question: how hard is computing a Boolean function?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the current state-of-the-art lower bounds are Ω(n) for explicit functions.

, in a nutshell, we have a trade-off between the average-case complexity and the size complexity of a Boolean function, where we have to pay a price of at least Ω̃ (k) ·s in the latter, in order to obtain a hardness of 1 2+2 −k in the former.
the current state of the art is that the best known lower bound on the size of the minimal formula that computes the AND function is O(n).
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we show that computing explicit functions requires larger formulas than approximating them.
we prove that if a function is hard to compute on average, it is hard to compute exactly.
we show a tradeoff between formula size and average-case hardness.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the complexity of approximating a function can be used to prove that it requires a large formula, even if the function is not explicitly known.
computing functions requires more resources (e.g. space or time) than approximating functions, even in the average-case.
the complexity of approximating a function can be much smaller than the complexity of computing it exactly.
